title: UNC788
summary: UNC788 is a provisional tracking label rather than the settled name of an established group. Vendors use the UNC prefix, alongside designations such as DEV, Storm, or TA, for clusters of activity that they can describe in technical detail but cannot yet connect to a known, named intrusion set, so such a label may later merge into another group or split into several separate ones. Those prefixes belong to the team that created them and are not shared standards, which is why two vendors can describe the same intrusion under two unrelated names. For a defender, the practical consequence is that a provisional label carries no reliable statement about sponsorship, motivation, or scope, and no campaign timeline. Treat such reporting as thin and likely to be revised, map whatever behaviour is published to techniques you can already detect, and keep your own telemetry as the primary evidence. Where public sources do not state a sponsor, record the gap instead of filling it with the nearest familiar name.

beginner.definition: UNC788 is a working name that security companies use for activity they have not fully identified. The letters UNC mean uncategorized, which simply means not yet sorted into a known group. Researchers can see the actions, but they cannot say for sure who is behind them. The name may change later when more evidence appears.
beginner.whyItMatters: Not every attacker has a famous name. Sometimes analysts see strange activity and cannot link it to anyone. They still publish a label so teams can talk about it and share warnings. If you treat the label as a fact, you may draw the wrong conclusion about who attacked you. The right approach is to focus on the behaviour you can see in your own logs.
howItWorks: Analysts notice a pattern of activity, such as logins from unusual places and times.
They compare it with known groups, but the details do not match well enough.
Instead of guessing a sponsor, they create a temporary label to name that activity.
Other teams use the label to share warnings and to compare their own findings.
As new evidence arrives, the label may merge with another group or split apart.
For defenders, the honest answer is often that the sponsor is still unknown.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital where several patients report the same unusual symptom. The doctors agree about what they see, but they cannot name the disease yet. They write a temporary label on the chart so every nurse knows what to watch for. The label is useful, but it is not a diagnosis. Later, more tests may show that two different illnesses were mixed together, or that a known disease explains all the cases. Treating the temporary label as the final answer would be a mistake.
takeaways: Treat provisional labels as questions, not as answers about who is attacking you.
Build detections from behaviour you observe, not from a group name.
Write down what you do not know, so your team does not fill the gap with guesses.

objectives: Explain what a provisional tracking label is and why vendors create one.
Describe how vendor naming conventions differ and why labels do not map cleanly between reports.
Explain how to convert thin cluster reporting into detections based on behaviour.
Identify the point at which a threat report should state that attribution is unknown.
Summarise how to write about an unattributed cluster without overstating the evidence.
